src/article/comment.entity.ts: `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn() id` and `@Column() body` define the database columns and key generation.
src/article/comment.entity.ts: `@ManyToOne(type => ArticleEntity, article => article.comments)` defines a relation between tables.

parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/article/comment.entity.ts is in the domain layer, but its only job is mapping the Comment table for TypeORM. `@Entity()` marks the class as a database table. `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn()` and `@Column()` define the database columns. `@ManyToOne(type => ArticleEntity, article => article.comments)` defines a relation between tables. All of this is persistence (infrastructure) work. The class has no domain behaviour, rules or checks of its own, so it acts as a persistence model rather than a domain entity. The call is close: the layer model puts all `*.entity.ts` files in the domain layer, which in NestJS projects usually means TypeORM entities, so the project may accept this on purpose. No ADR prose says so, and the rubric names persistence work in a domain file as a failure. Confidence is therefore moderate.
